before.note: Read Databases first, since a storage engine is the part of a database that stores its rows. Indexing helps but is not needed: this page explains B-trees from the start.

stages.name: Basics
body: A storage engine is the part of a database that keeps rows on disk and finds them again. MySQL makes the idea visible: it ships several engines, and its SHOW ENGINES statement lists the engines a server knows, whether each is available, and which one is the default [[mysql-engines]].

Disks read and write in blocks, so engines group data into fixed-size pages. PostgreSQL stores each table and index as an array of fixed-size pages, usually 8 kB [[pg-page]]. InnoDB's default index page is 16 KB [[mysql-physical]]. Changing one row means rewriting the page that holds it, and that single fact explains many of the costs later in this page.

The classic structure for finding a page quickly is the B-tree, a balanced tree of sorted pages. PostgreSQL describes its btree index as a multi-way balanced tree that can index any data type that sorts into a well-defined linear order [[pg-btree]]. That the tree stays shallow, so a lookup touches only a few pages, is general knowledge rather than something that page spells out.

terms.definition: The part of a database that decides how rows are stored on disk and how they are found and changed.
A fixed-size chunk of a file, such as 8 kB or 16 KB, that a B-tree engine reads and writes as a unit.
A balanced tree of sorted pages, so any key is found by walking from the root down to one leaf page.
Changing data by rewriting the page where it already lives.

stages.name: How it works
body: A second design avoids editing files at all. RocksDB's overview names three parts: the memtable, an in-memory structure that takes new writes; the logfile, a sequentially written file that records them; and sorted files on disk. When the memtable fills up it is flushed to a sorted file, and the matching log can be deleted [[rocks-overview]].

Cassandra's documentation lists the same path in order: log the write in the commit log, write it to the memtable, flush the memtable, and store the data on disk in SSTables. It says the engine is built on log-structured merge (LSM) trees, which append instead of using the B-trees of traditional relational databases [[cass-storage]].

LevelDB's notes give concrete sizes. Its log turns into a sorted table at about 4 MB by default, and a copy of the log lives in memory as the memtable, which is consulted on every read [[leveldb-impl]]. RocksDB's memtable defaults to 64 MB, is a skip list unless you change it, and becomes read-only when it fills while a background thread flushes it [[rocks-memtable]].

A read has to look at more than one place. RocksDB's memtable page says the memtable is read before the sorted files because its data is newer [[rocks-memtable]]. The consequence is that an LSM-tree trades some read work for cheap, sequential writes.

terms.definition: The sorted in-memory buffer where an LSM-tree puts new writes.
A file that records each write before it is applied, so memory can be rebuilt after a crash.
A sorted, immutable file produced when a memtable is flushed.
A design that appends writes, keeps sorted immutable files and merges them in the background.
Writing a full memtable out to disk as a sorted file.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Sorted files pile up, so engines merge them. RocksDB's leveled compaction keeps a special level 0 of freshly flushed files, and every deeper level is one sorted run split into files. Each deeper level has a target size, and the targets grow exponentially. When level 0 has enough files they are merged into level 1, and when a level grows past its target a file is merged into the overlapping files of the next level [[rocks-leveled]].

LevelDB's notes give a worked example. Level 0 is merged into level 1 when it exceeds four files; level 1 holds up to 10 MB, level 2 up to 100 MB, and so on. Merges use only bulk reads and writes, which avoids slow seeks [[leveldb-impl]]. The same notes explain that a delete is stored as a marker that hides older values in older tables, so deleted data lingers until a merge removes it [[leveldb-impl]].

Reads stay fast with help. RocksDB can put a Bloom filter in every sorted file, a bit array that tells the engine a file may contain a key or definitely does not. At 9.9 bits per key the page quotes a 1% false positive rate, meaning one file in a hundred is checked for nothing [[rocks-bloom]].

The B-tree side has limits too. PostgreSQL notes an index entry cannot exceed about one third of a page [[pg-btree]], and InnoDB deliberately leaves a share of each page free so later inserts have room [[mysql-physical]].

terms.definition: A group of sorted files in an LSM-tree; deeper levels are larger and hold older data.
Merging sorted files into new ones, dropping overwritten and deleted entries.
A delete marker that hides older versions of a key until compaction removes both.
A compact summary that says a key is definitely absent or maybe present, so a file can be skipped.
How full a B-tree page is left when it is built, leaving room for later inserts.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: Every engine pays somewhere. Cassandra's documentation says compaction is a necessary background activity for the merge phase of an LSM-tree, and that it creates write amplification: small files are read, merged and a new file is written, so every write is rewritten several times and adds background I/O [[cass-storage]].

A B-tree pays in a different place. InnoDB leaves one sixteenth of a page free for later inserts. Rows inserted in order leave pages about 15/16 full, but rows inserted in random order leave pages anywhere from half to 15/16 full [[mysql-physical]]. That unused space is the cost of updating in place.

So the decision depends on the workload. Many writes and a need to save space point towards an LSM-tree; read-mostly work with range scans and lookups by key points towards a B-tree. The two company posts on the topic page show exactly this: one team moved from a B-tree to an LSM-tree to save space, and another found what an LSM-tree costs to operate.
To explore, MySQL's SHOW ENGINES shows what a server supports [[mysql-engines]], and RocksDB's ldb tool lets you write and read a tiny database from a shell [[rocks-ldb]].

misconceptions.myth: LSM-trees are only good at writes and are bad at reads.
misconceptions.truth: A read may check several places, but engines add Bloom filters so most sorted files are skipped, and they read the memtable first because its data is newer [[rocks-bloom]] [[rocks-memtable]].

misconceptions.myth: A B-tree engine updates in place, so it never wastes space.
misconceptions.truth: InnoDB leaves part of each page free for later inserts, and pages built from random inserts are anywhere from half full to 15/16 full [[mysql-physical]].
Cassandra's documentation calls compaction a necessary background activity for the merge phase of an LSM-tree, and notes that it creates write amplification [[cass-storage]].

misconceptions.myth: Deleting a key frees its space at once.
misconceptions.truth: In LevelDB a delete is stored as a marker that hides older values in older tables, so the data stays until a merge removes it [[leveldb-impl]].
